record.original_question: Study the hyper abundant numbers: integers N for which there is a real parameter u such that, for every integer M >= 1, sigma(M) / (M (log M)^u) <= sigma(N) / (N (log N)^u), where sigma(n) is the sum of divisors of n. Can the methods used by Guy Robin for hyper composite numbers be adapted to obtain structural or counting results for these hyper abundant numbers?

evidence.quote: Probably, the method used by G. Robin in [39] can be adapted to study hyper abundant numbers
but, as far as I know, nobody did it.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\sigma(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d$ denote the sum-of-divisors function. Call a positive integer $N$ a *hyper abundant number* if there exists a real number $u$ (depending on $N$) such that
$$\frac{\sigma(M)}{M(\log M)^{u}}\;\le\;\frac{\sigma(N)}{N(\log N)^{u}}\qquad\text{for every integer }M\ge 2.$$
(That is, $N$ maximizes $M\mapsto \sigma(M)/(M(\log M)^{u})$ for some choice of $u$.)

Develop structural and counting results for the set of hyper abundant numbers, in analogy with the theory of "hyper composite" (highly composite / superabundant / colossally abundant) numbers developed by G. Robin. In particular:

(a) Describe the prime factorization structure of hyper abundant numbers (e.g., whether they are of the form $\prod_{p\le P}p^{a_p}$ with non-increasing exponents).
(b) Give an asymptotic formula, or non-trivial upper and lower bounds, for the counting function $Q(x) = \#\{N\le x : N \text{ is hyper abundant}\}$.
(c) Determine to what extent Robin-type methods (used for colossally abundant and related extremal numbers in the study of $\sigma(n)/(n\log\log n)$) can be transferred to this weighted maximization problem with $(\log M)^u$ in place of $\log\log M$.
artifact.status_search_result: Standard references discuss highly abundant, superabundant, and colossally abundant numbers (Alaoglu–Erdős, Robin) and Robin's inequality relating $\sigma(n)/(n\log\log n)$ to the Riemann hypothesis, but no readily available source treats the specific "hyper abundant" notion defined via maximization of $\sigma(M)/(M(\log M)^u)$, nor adapts Robin's method to it. The status appears unknown / not addressed in the published literature accessible by search.

status_evidence.title: Colossally abundant number - Wikipedia
status_evidence.snippet: Robin's inequality, if it ever fails to hold, will fail for a colossally abundant number n; thus the Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to Robin's inequality holding for every colossally abundant number.
status_evidence.claim: Robin's method targets the maximizers of sigma(n)/(n log log n); the (log M)^u weighting in the proposed 'hyper abundant' definition is not covered by these standard treatments.

status_evidence.title: Superabundant numbers, their subsequences and the Riemann hypothesis
status_evidence.snippet: Study of superabundant numbers and subsequences in relation to Robin's inequality.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work continues to investigate variants of extremal sigma-maximizing sequences, but the specific 'hyper abundant' variant described above does not appear in accessible literature.
